text: Now we actually build the piece that turns thirty-one flat CSV files into something Athena can query: a Glue Crawler. This lesson walks through the real setup, step by step, starting from an empty Glue Data Catalog.

First, the crawler needs somewhere to register a table, called a Glue database — which is just a logical namespace in the Catalog, not a running database engine. We create one called northfield_raw_db to hold Northfield's raw, uncataloged exports.

Next, the crawler needs permission to do its job, and only its job. The role AWSGlueServiceRole-NorthfieldCapstone gets read-only access scoped to the northfield-raw-zone bucket, plus permission to read and write the Glue Catalog — nothing more. It can't touch Redshift, delete S3 objects, or reach any other bucket in the account. Least privilege matters even on a small project.

With the database and role in place, we create the crawler itself, named northfield-orders-raw-crawler, pointed at the exact prefix from Lesson 3: s3 colon slash slash northfield-raw-zone slash orders-raw. Then we start it. It moves through four stages — starting, running, stopping, ready — sampling the files and inferring their schema. For thirty-one small CSV files, that's well under a minute.

One detail worth calling out: this crawler runs on demand, triggered by hand, once — not on a schedule. Glue Crawlers can absolutely run on a cron-style schedule, and that's exactly what the automated version of this pipeline uses once ingestion happens every day. But this is a one-time August export. Scheduling a crawler against data that never changes would just cost a little for no benefit.

When the crawler finishes, it creates a table — named orders_raw, after the S3 prefix folder, which is Glue's default naming convention. Next lesson, we dig into exactly what schema it inferred, and where it got something not quite right.
